stem: Which of these are fundamental principles of British life? Select TWO.
options: Following one national religion
Tolerance of other faiths and beliefs
Individual liberty
Loyalty to one political party
explanation: Individual liberty and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs are core principles. The UK has no single compulsory party or religion.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: Which phrase best describes the principle of individual liberty?
options: Freedom to ignore any laws you personally disagree with
A right to be given a job by the state
Freedom to make your own choices within the law
A duty to follow your family's religion
explanation: Individual liberty means people can choose how to live their lives, as long as they stay within the law.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: Which of these are responsibilities that people living in the UK should accept? Select TWO.
options: Treating others with fairness
Agreeing with every government policy
Looking after yourself and your family
Speaking only English in your home
explanation: Treating others fairly and looking after yourself and your family are both expected. You may disagree with the government and use any language at home.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: A neighbour strongly disagrees with your political views. What does British life expect you to do?
options: Respect their right to hold their view
Report them to the police
Ask the council to warn them
Insist that they change their view
explanation: Everyone has the right to their own opinion, and respecting that right is one of the responsibilities of living in the UK.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: Which right does everyone in the UK have if they are accused of a crime?
options: The right to choose their judge
The right to a fair trial
The right to be tried in their country of birth
The right to a trial without a judge
explanation: A fair trial is one of the freedoms guaranteed to everyone living in the UK.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: Freedom of speech means you can say anything in the UK, including threats of violence, without breaking the law.
options: True
False
explanation: Free speech is protected, but it works within the law. Threatening violence or stirring up hatred can be a crime.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: At a citizenship ceremony, what is the difference between the oath and the affirmation?
options: The affirmation is only for children
The oath is spoken and the affirmation is sung
The oath is made to Parliament and the affirmation to the monarch
The oath mentions God and the affirmation does not
explanation: People who wish to swear by God take the oath. Those who prefer a non-religious promise make a solemn affirmation instead.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: In the citizenship pledge, new citizens promise to do which of these? Select TWO.
options: Vote at every election
Live in the UK for the rest of their lives
Uphold the UK's democratic values
Observe its laws faithfully
explanation: The pledge covers respecting rights and freedoms, upholding democratic values, observing the laws and fulfilling the duties of a citizen. Voting is not compulsory.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: What does indefinite leave to remain allow a person to do?
options: Live in the UK permanently
Hold a British passport
Visit the UK for up to six months
Vote in every UK election
explanation: Indefinite leave to remain, often called settlement, gives permission to live in the UK permanently. Citizenship and a British passport are a separate step.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK

stem: Once you have indefinite leave to remain, you automatically become a British citizen.
options: True
False
explanation: Settlement lets you live in the UK permanently. Becoming a citizen is a separate application, usually made later.
source: Handbook ch. 1 · The values and principles of the UK
